title_original: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
excerpt_original: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly…

blocks.text: I n the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.
Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

blocks.alt: ​A man works with tools on a large block of wood in the bow of a large wooden boat. Another man sits behind him
blocks.caption: A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy

blocks.text: The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today.

blocks.alt: The timber frame of a large wooden boat mid-construction sits next to a body of water
blocks.caption: The huge teak dhows, traditional vessels suited to long voyages across the Indian Ocean, take about three years to build

blocks.alt: A man works with tools on the wooden interior of a boat
A man’s body can be seen sitting on a beam holding a large torque wrench
A smiling man stands on a ladder holding a hammer
blocks.caption: Clockwise from top left: a worker cuts a varangue, part of the boat’s frame, from a large piece of teak. This piece connects the two sides of the hull to the keel; a bolt securing a beam to a boat’s frame is tightened; using a chain hoist, a worker positions a stemson inside the hull of a boat; a worker heads home on Thursday evening. The following day, Friday, is the weekly rest day.

blocks.text: It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai.

After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation.

blocks.alt: Four men watch while another man wearing a welding mask carries out some welding on a large metal boat
blocks.caption: Workers in Manvi also maintain and repair modern vessels

blocks.text: The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition.

Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical.
Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals.

blocks.caption: The local beach is a popular entertainment spot
